question: For seven years, the Commission and GRECO have been calling on Spain to effectively regulate interest groups, be more transparent and tighten the rules on incompatibilities for senior and former policymakers.

The absence of a regulatory framework for lobbying has helped create an environment that is institutionally opaque and leads to serious cases such as the current scandal affecting former Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, which includes alleged oil businesses, trading gold, business with risky companies such as Huawei, as well as the collection of possible kickbacks and money laundering.
In light of the above: 1.

In the Commission’s view, does this case reflect risks in terms of institutionalised corruption, transparency and control of political influence that the Commission and GRECO have been highlighting as points of concern for Spain for several years?

Does the Commission intend to step up the specific follow-up on Spain in the next rule of law report in the light of the judicial investigations into the ‘Zapatero case’, particularly as a result of alleged schemes of influence peddling, money laundering and economic considerations linked to third countries with high risks in terms of corruption and democratic standards, such as Venezuela and China?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) The Commission does not comment on individual cases. The Commission closely follows the developments in all Member States, including Spain, as regards the rule of law and anti-corruption efforts, notably under the annual Rule of Law Report. The seventh EU Rule of Law report was published on 17 July 20261.

Regarding anti-corruption, the Commission concluded in the 2026 Report that Spain has made limited progress on the recommendations on lobbying and on the rules on conflicts of interest and asset declarations of persons in top executive functions, as well as some progress on the recommendation on addressing the length of investigations and prosecutions of high-level corruption.

The Commission recommended Spain to continue the ongoing procedure to adopt legislation on lobbying, including the establishment of a mandatory public register of lobbyists, to strengthen rules on conflicts of interest and asset declarations of persons with top executive functions, and to take forward the legislative process to revise the Code of Criminal Procedure to strengthen the framework for investigations and prosecutions in high-level corruption cases, with a view to reducing delays.
